title: Adaptive Conformal Anomaly Detection with Time Series Foundation Models
one_liner: Turn a pre-trained time series model's predictions into honest, self-updating anomaly alarms that work when the data drifts.
lead: When a sensor starts behaving strangely, how do you know if it is broken or just following a new pattern? Foundation models (big pre-trained time series brains) make good guesses, but they do not tell you how confident they are or whether to raise an alarm. This paper wraps those guesses in a guard rail that works without retraining, updates itself as new data arrives, and tells you the honest false-alarm rate of every threshold you pick.

problem.h2: The gap between model guesses and honest alarms
paras: Time series foundation models are like excellent weather forecasters — they make predictions, but they never tell you their exact confidence level. In anomaly detection (spotting when a machine is about to break, or a sensor went haywire), you need to say yes or no: is this reading unusual enough to trigger an alarm?

A naive approach: pick a fixed threshold on the model's error. Sounds simple. But data drifts — a sensor calibrates, a factory changes its routine, a city enters winter. The same error size might have meant broken yesterday and normal today. And you never actually know the false alarm rate of your threshold; it is a guess.
The paper shows that without updating your alarm calibration as new data arrives, false alarms either skyrocket or anomalies slip through.

callout.html: After a foundation model predicts, use conformal prediction (a math tool that builds honest confidence bounds) with adaptive weights that learn from past predictions to keep false alarms constant even as data drifts.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the error threshold
paras: Normally you pick a fixed threshold: if prediction error exceeds this number, raise an alarm. The paper makes that threshold adaptive — it learns from recent history which errors are normal and shifts smoothly as the data changes (the pattern of readings the sensor produces).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: false alarm rate
hidden.name: the false alarm rate (p-value)
paras: A false alarm is when the threshold triggers but nothing is actually wrong. The paper measures how often this happens — not as a guess, but as a proven statistical guarantee. Conformal prediction is a mathematical trick that says: if you use past errors to build a bound, and you ask for 95% coverage, the math guarantees you will not exceed 5% false alarms on truly normal data.

The adaptive part learns which past errors to trust as you see new data. Errors from a week ago when the sensor was in a different state get downweighted. Errors from yesterday stay high weight. The paper estimates these weights by tracking how useful each past error was in predicting today's error size.

heat.caption: Darker means higher weight. Recent big errors influence the threshold more; old small errors less.

reads.html: The false alarm rate is just: out of all the times you call anomaly when things are fine, what fraction is that? You want to control it — say, no more than 5%. Conformal prediction is a recipe for building alarms with a mathematical proof that you stay under your target rate.

Conformal prediction (Vovk et al.) gives marginal coverage guarantees: if the past errors are independent and identically distributed, the coverage is at least 1−alpha. The adaptive conformal method replaces that assumption with adaptive weighting — a weighted quantile of past errors shifts the bound as the data pattern changes, and the weights are learned online from residual regression.

mechanism.h2: Why adaptive weighting keeps false alarms honest
paras: Here is the chain: A foundation model is trained on tons of data (e.g. historical sensor readings). It makes a guess for today. The guess is wrong by some amount — the error. Normally you would use the distribution of all past errors to set your alarm threshold. But if the sensor drifted (the data changed), old errors are misleading. Weighting old errors less fixes that.

The math: a weighted quantile of past errors gives you a threshold. If you ask for the 95th percentile of weighted errors, then roughly 95% of weighted past errors fall below it. Now comes the genius part: if you choose the weights using past data (not peeking at today), the conformal theory still guarantees that future new errors will exceed the threshold at most 5% of the time. No retraining needed. The weights adapt by regression (fitting a small model that predicts today's error size from the weights of yesterday's errors). As the sensor drifts, the best weights shift, the threshold shifts, and false alarms stay controlled.

math.words: threshold at time t equals the weighted quantile of past errors, where weights decay by age and adapt by regression
math.equation: Q_t(1−alpha) = quantile_{w_t}(E_{1..t-1}), where w_t learned from residuals of E_t on w_{t-1}

the weighted quantile using weights w_t

bars.h2: False alarm rate: fixed vs. adaptive

charts.title: Fixed threshold (fails on drift)
charts.note: Fixed threshold ignores drift. False alarm rate climbs as data changes.

charts.title: Adaptive conformal (this paper)
charts.note: Weights adapt. False alarm rate stays near target (5%) even as foundation model sees new data patterns.

items.html: If you have only 20 past errors but want to build a 95th percentile, the quantile is noisy. The method works best with hundreds or thousands of past predictions to estimate quantiles reliably.

If the data changes faster than the weight adaptation learns, the weights stay tuned to old conditions. The threshold stays too loose (catches anomalies that are now normal) or too tight (misses real anomalies in the new state), because the weights have not yet shifted to match today's errors. The method assumes data drifts gradually enough that yesterday's error history is relevant today.
If a real anomaly happens and creates a large error, the weights might upweight it, making future similar errors less anomalous. The paper assumes anomalies are rare.
With sufficient historical data and gradual drift, the method delivers a threshold with a mathematical false alarm guarantee, adapts automatically, and never retrains the foundation model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic time series that drifts slowly (e.g. the mean shifts, or the variance grows). Feed it to a small pre-trained foundation model (or mock one with a noisy linear predictor). Run three alarm strategies: (1) fixed threshold on raw errors, (2) fixed conformal (no adaptation), (3) adaptive conformal (this paper). Measure false alarm rate and detection rate (true positives) on a clean drifting section and a section with real anomalies injected.
demo.closing: The demo should show: (1) fixed threshold fails as data drifts; (2) adaptive conformal keeps false alarms near your target even with drift; (3) detection rate stays high because the threshold is built from actual error distribution, not blind guessing.
